expectedText:
WORK MADE FOR HIRE AGREEMENT (INDEPENDENT CONTRACTOR)
Prepared for Acme, Inc.

WHO OWNS COPYRIGHT BY DEFAULT IN A CONTRACTOR RELATIONSHIP
Under federal copyright law, copyright in a work vests initially in the person who actually creates it — the author — the moment the work is fixed in a tangible form. When Jordan Lee creates A bronze sculpture titled ‘Pacific Light,’ installed in the plaza in 2015. for Acme, Inc. as an independent contractor rather than as an employee, Jordan Lee is, by default, both the author and the copyright owner of that work, even though Acme, Inc. commissioned and paid for it. That default changes only if the work qualifies as a “work made for hire” under federal copyright law's specific definition of that term, or if Jordan Lee separately assigns ownership to Acme, Inc. in a signed writing.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Copyright in a work protected under this title vests initially in the author or authors of the work. The authors of a joint work are coowners of copyright in the work."
  — 17 U.S.C. § 201(a) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, initial ownership of copyright (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/201)
  "In the case of a work made for hire, the employer or other person for whom the work was prepared is considered the author for purposes of this title, and, unless the parties have expressly agreed otherwise in a written instrument signed by them, owns all of the rights comprised in the copyright."
  — 17 U.S.C. § 201(b) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, ownership of work made for hire (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/201)
  "As a general rule, the author is the party who actually creates the work, that is, the person who translates an idea into a fixed, tangible expression entitled to copyright protection."
  — Community for Creative Non-Violence v. Reid, 490 U.S. 730, 737 (1989) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/112273/community-for-creative-non-violence-v-reid/)
  Known gap: This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section (17 U.S.C. § 201(a) and § 201(b)); no additional independent source was found for this point beyond the statute itself and the Supreme Court's own restatement of it, since both subsections describe the same initial-ownership rule and its work-for-hire exception. This is federal law, used as real evidence of how copyright ownership is allocated by default between an independent creator and the party that commissioned the work — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs a reader's specific situation, or about whether any particular work or relationship actually qualifies as independent-contractor work under this rule.

THE STATUTORY DEFINITION OF “WORK MADE FOR HIRE” HAS TWO SEPARATE BRANCHES
Federal copyright law defines “work made for hire” in exactly two ways: work created by an employee within the scope of employment, or work that is both specially ordered or commissioned for use in one of nine enumerated categories — a contribution to a collective work, a part of a motion picture or other audiovisual work, a translation, a supplementary work, a compilation, an instructional text, a test, answer material for a test, or an atlas — and made the subject of an express written agreement, signed by both parties, that the work is a work made for hire. Work Jordan Lee creates for Acme, Inc. as an independent contractor, rather than as an employee, can only ever fall within the second of these two definitions; the first branch applies only to an actual employment relationship as federal law defines it, a status independent contractor status is legally distinct from.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "A “work made for hire” is— (1) a work prepared by an employee within the scope of his or her employment; or (2) a work specially ordered or commissioned for use as a contribution to a collective work, as a part of a motion picture or other audiovisual work, as a translation, as a supplementary work, as a compilation, as an instructional text, as a test, as answer material for a test, or as an atlas, if the parties expressly agree in a written instrument signed by them that the work shall be considered a work made for hire."
  — 17 U.S.C. § 101 (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, definition of “work made for hire” (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/101)
  Known gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of how the two branches of the “work made for hire” definition are structured — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs a reader's specific situation, or about whether the contractor's relationship with the hiring party named in this agreement is, in fact, an independent-contractor relationship rather than an employment relationship (a separate, fact-specific question this clause does not resolve). This clause quotes the same statutory text (17 U.S.C. § 101) already quoted elsewhere in this project's corpus, in this project's Invention Assignment & Confidentiality Agreement and Copyright Assignment Agreement documents; it is repeated here, in a document specifically about the independent-contractor branch of the definition, because that document's own framing centers on the employee branch and does not itself state the independent-contractor branch's requirements.

WORK-FOR-HIRE STATUS FOR A CONTRACTOR DOES NOT ARISE AUTOMATICALLY
Unlike the employee branch of the work-made-for-hire doctrine, the independent-contractor branch does not attach automatically just because Acme, Inc. hired Jordan Lee to create A bronze sculpture titled ‘Pacific Light,’ installed in the plaza in 2015. and paid for it. Both of two separate conditions have to be satisfied: the work has to actually fall within one of the statute's nine enumerated categories, and the parties have to expressly agree, in a written instrument signed by both of them, that the work is a work made for hire. If either condition is missing, the work is not a “work made for hire” under federal law — regardless of what a contract calls it, what the parties intended, or how the parties otherwise describe their working relationship.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Sculpture does not fit within any of the nine categories of “specially ordered or commissioned” works enumerated in that subsection, and no written agreement between the parties establishes “Third World America” as a work for hire."
  — Community for Creative Non-Violence v. Reid, 490 U.S. 730, 738 (1989) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/112273/community-for-creative-non-violence-v-reid/)
  "Because Reid was an independent contractor, whether “Third World America” is a work for hire depends on whether it satisfies the terms of § 101(2). This petitioners concede it cannot do. Thus, CCNV is not the author of “Third World America” by virtue of the work for hire provisions of the Act."
  — Community for Creative Non-Violence v. Reid, 490 U.S. 730, 753 (1989) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/112273/community-for-creative-non-violence-v-reid/)
  Known gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of how the independent-contractor branch of the work-made-for-hire definition actually functions when applied — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs a reader's specific situation, or about whether any particular commissioned work satisfies these conditions. Both citations below are drawn from the same Supreme Court opinion (different passages of it), applying the statute to the facts before the Court; that opinion is also cited elsewhere in this project's corpus for a related but distinct point (the common-law agency factors used to decide who counts as an “employee” under the first branch), which this clause does not repeat.

WORK MADE FOR HIRE DESIGNATION
Jordan Lee and Acme, Inc. agree that A bronze sculpture titled ‘Pacific Light,’ installed in the plaza in 2015. is specially ordered and commissioned by Acme, Inc., that it falls within the following category under 17 U.S.C. § 101: part of an audiovisual work, and that it shall be considered a “work made for hire” as that term is defined under federal copyright law. This designation is made in the written instrument signed by both parties below.

WORK OUTSIDE THE NINE CATEGORIES CAN STILL BE TRANSFERRED BY A SEPARATE ASSIGNMENT
Work commissioned from an independent contractor that does not fall within one of the statute's nine enumerated categories cannot become Acme, Inc.'s property through a “work made for hire” designation, no matter how an agreement describes it — federal law does not let parties expand the nine categories by private agreement. That does not mean ownership of such work is stuck with Jordan Lee regardless of the parties' intentions, though: federal law separately allows a contractor to transfer copyright ownership to the hiring party through an ordinary assignment, which is valid as long as it is set out in a signed writing. A work-for-hire clause that does not legally qualify as a work-for-hire designation is not, for that reason alone, void or without effect — when the same agreement also includes assignment language, that language can still operate as a valid transfer of ownership.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "A transfer of copyright ownership, other than by operation of law, is not valid unless an instrument of conveyance, or a note or memorandum of the transfer, is in writing and signed by the owner of the rights conveyed or such owner’s duly authorized agent."
  — 17 U.S.C. § 204(a) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, execution of transfers of copyright ownership (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/204)
  "The rule is really quite simple: If the copyright holder agrees to transfer ownership to another party, that party must get the copyright holder to sign a piece of paper saying so. It doesn't have to be the Magna Charta; a one-line pro forma statement will do."
  — Effects Associates, Inc. v. Cohen, 908 F.2d 555 (9th Cir. 1990) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/544754/effects-associates-inc-v-larry-cohen/)
  Known gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of how a signed writing actually transfers copyright ownership, separately from (and as a backstop to) any work-for-hire designation — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs a reader's specific situation, or that any particular contract's language is effective to accomplish either an assignment or a work-for-hire designation, which depends on the document's actual wording. The Effects Associates quote below is reused, not independently re-verified in this research session, from this project's already-verified Copyright Assignment Agreement document (checked 2026-09-01): CourtListener's search tool returned a daily rate-limit error ("429 — Rate limit exceeded: 125/day") when this research attempted to re-fetch it directly, so that specific citation is disclosed as reused rather than freshly re-confirmed this session. The 17 U.S.C. § 204(a) statutory quote below, by contrast, was independently fetched and verified fresh in this research session. Effects Associates is Ninth Circuit precedent; it is frequently cited nationally on this point but is only binding within that circuit.

BACKUP ASSIGNMENT OF OWNERSHIP
To the extent A bronze sculpture titled ‘Pacific Light,’ installed in the plaza in 2015. is determined not to qualify as a “work made for hire” under federal copyright law — whether because it does not fall within one of the statutory categories described above, because the designation above is found deficient for any reason, or otherwise — Jordan Lee hereby assigns to Acme, Inc. all right, title, and interest in and to the copyright in A bronze sculpture titled ‘Pacific Light,’ installed in the plaza in 2015., effective as of the date this agreement is signed. Jordan Lee agrees to sign any additional documents reasonably requested by Acme, Inc. to confirm, record, or perfect this assignment.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
Please sign below to indicate agreement to the terms above.

Contractor: Jordan Lee
Date: _______________

Company: Acme, Inc.
